newsitem.title: USA: Jurors begin deliberations in du Pont murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Jurors begin deliberations in du Pont murder trial.

text.p: Jurors began deliberations on Tuesday in the murder trial of chemicals heir John du Pont, accused of killing Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz at the millionaire's sprawling suburban Philadelphia estate.

Just before the jury of six men and six women entered sequestration to begin their deliberations, they were told in closing arguments by defence and prosecution attorneys to decide if du Pont knew what he was doing was wrong in killing Schultz on Jan. 26, 1996.

Defence attorney Thomas Bergstrom, comparing du Pont's mental state to a waking nightmare, said evidence presented over 13 days of testimony showed du Pont was driven to kill by delusions caused by long-standing paranoid schizophrenia.

But lead prosecutor Joseph McGettigan said du Pont was driven by anger and resentment rather than legal insanity to kill Schultz and arrogantly believed his wealth and influence would allow him to escape the consequences.

"Anger doesn't mean out of touch with reality," McGettigan said, adding that Schultz was killed "because an arrogant person took the most arrogant act a human being could take." Du Pont had become increasingly angry with Schultz, who he believed was threatening his position within the wrestling world, McGettigan added.
Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins delivered final instructions to the jury following closing arguments.

Jurors can render verdicts of guilty, not guilty, not guilty by reason of insanity, or guilty but mentally ill, which carries the same punishment as a guilty verdict but allows a convicted person to obtain treatment first.
Albert Allen, one of the alternate jurors, told reporters he thought du Pont was guilty but mentally ill. He said he thought the jury "would do the right thing."
Du Pont also is charged with simple assault in allegedly pointing a gun at witnesses Nancy Schultz -- David Schultz's widow -- and Patrick Goodale, a security consultant hired by du Pont.
Du Pont, 58, sat impassively, as he has throughout the trial, as both lawyers in their closing arguments agreed he was mentally ill and killed Schultz.

Failure to know the wrongfulness of one's act is a key criterion for an insanity defence. Bergstrom, arguing for an insanity verdict, asked jurors to compare their own brief moments of night-time terrors with what he said was a paranoia and fear that gripped du Pont constantly.
This led him to acts such as lining the walls of his house with razor wire and digging up the grounds of his estate looking for the corpse of an imagined chambermaid he believed was his mother.
"Imagine having those nightmares in the light of day ... If you do, I think you'll understand what's in the mind of the defendant," Bergstrom said.
